articles.title: Lucien Rezende (PSOL): regionalizar saúde e 20 delegacias das mulheres | G1
articles.standfirst: A jornalista Bruna Mendes conduziu entrevista com o candidato ao governo de Mato Grosso do Sul, direto dos estúdios da TV Morena.
articles.summary: A jornalista Bruna Mendes conduziu entrevista com o candidato ao governo de Mato Grosso do Sul, direto dos estúdios da TV Morena.
articles.body:
Lucien Rezende (PSOL) é entrevistado no MS1. — Foto: Débora Ricalde/g1 MS

O candidato Lucien Rezende (PSOL) é o último candidato ao governo de Mato Grosso do Sul a ser entrevistado nesta sexta-feira (18), durante o MSTV 1ª edição. A conversa ao vivo foi conduzida pela jornalista Bruna Mendes. Assista à íntegra da entrevista no vídeo acima.

Entre os temas abordados estiveram saúde, segurança pública, educação, economia, assistência social, meio ambiente e agricultura. Veja, abaixo, as respostas de Lucien Rezende sobre cada assunto.

A entrevista faz parte de uma série de sabatinas ao vivo com candidatos ao governo de Mato Grosso do Sul. A TV Morena promoveu reuniões com os partidos políticos para definir a ordem das entrevistas com os candidatos ao governo do estado na emissora.

Confira o que respondeu o candidato sobre os seguintes temas:

Primeira pergunta: Regionalização da saúde

O candidato afirmou que os recursos investidos atualmente na saúde são insuficientes. Segundo ele, a regionalização do atendimento pode ajudar a reduzir as filas, mas é preciso ampliar a estrutura para colocar os projetos em prática.

Segundo o candidato, os atendimentos de alta complexidade acabam concentrados em Campo Grande, o que obriga moradores do interior a viajar para a capital. A proposta é ampliar a estrutura regional, com destaque para a criação de um polo em Miranda, que atende municípios da região. Ele também defende a construção de hospitais de excelência no interior para reduzir os deslocamentos.

Segundo pergunta: Ampliar recursos na saúde

O candidato citou dados divulgados pela imprensa sobre os investimentos em saúde no estado e afirmou que Mato Grosso do Sul aplica 8% dos recursos, enquanto a legislação prevê um percentual de até 12%.

Para ele, existe uma diferença entre os números apresentados sobre a saúde do estado e a realidade enfrentada pela população, principalmente em relação ao acesso a exames.

Terceira pergunta: Projeto 'Saúde em Casa'

O candidato afirmou que pretende implementar um modelo de atendimento domiciliar inspirado em uma experiência de Pernambuco durante a gestão de Eduardo Campos.

Entre as propostas está a utilização de unidades de terapia intensiva (UTIs) móveis no interior para atender os municípios e evitar que idosos precisem se deslocar até postos de saúde para receber atendimento.

Quarta pergunta: 20 novas delegacias das mulheres e segurança pública

O candidato afirmou que pretende ampliar as políticas de combate à violência contra a mulher. Segundo ele, Mato Grosso do Sul apresenta índices elevados de agressões e, apesar da existência das Salas Lilás, faltam delegacias especializadas para o atendimento feminino.

A proposta é começar a implantação de cerca de 20 delegacias. Ele também defendeu a ampliação do aluguel social por um ano ou mais para oferecer suporte financeiro às mulheres vítimas de violência. Para o candidato, a redução da desigualdade, por meio de políticas sociais e da educação em tempo integral, também pode contribuir para diminuir a violência.

O candidato afirmou que o combate à criminalidade deve começar pela ampliação das oportunidades de estudo, qualificação e trabalho. Segundo ele, jovens negros e moradores de periferias estão entre os grupos mais atingidos pelo encarceramento. A proposta apresentada é atuar nas causas sociais para reduzir o número de pessoas presas.

Quinta pergunta: Combate ao crime organizado e encarceramento

O candidato destacou o trabalho das polícias Civil e Militar e afirmou que a contratação de novos profissionais também é necessária para reforçar a segurança.

Ele citou um concurso com 400 policiais que, segundo ele, ainda não foram chamados pelo atual governo. Para o sistema prisional, defendeu a construção de mais duas ou até quatro unidades nos grandes centros, após diálogo com a secretaria responsável.

Sexta pergunta: Escolas em tempo integral

A proposta é ampliar o número de escolas com ensino em tempo integral nos 79 municípios de Mato Grosso do Sul.

O candidato afirmou que considera a medida um investimento, e não um custo. Ele também citou os recursos provenientes de empreendimentos instalados no estado como uma possível fonte para financiar as ações e outras políticas, como a construção de casas para idosos.

Sétima pergunta: Equiparação de salários de professores

O candidato não apresentou um número específico. Ele defendeu a realização de concursos públicos e a equiparação salarial dos profissionais da educação.

Também afirmou que pretende dialogar com a categoria para melhorar a qualificação e a remuneração dos professores.

Oitava pergunta: Cursos profissionalizantes para ampliar mão de obra

O candidato afirmou que falta planejamento do estado para lidar com os trabalhadores que atuam temporariamente nas grandes obras. Segundo ele, o governo sabia desde 2010 que os empreendimentos seriam instalados, mas não teria preparado mão de obra para atender à nova demanda.

A proposta é acelerar a formação profissional para as oportunidades geradas pelas fábricas em municípios como Inocência e Bataguassu. Ele citou a Universidade Estadual de Mato Grosso do Sul (UEMS) como uma ferramenta para oferecer formação, inclusive a distância.

Nona pergunta: Recursos para infraestrutura

O candidato afirmou que os impactos provocados pela expansão da logística já eram conhecidos, mas que não houve planejamento suficiente. Sobre a Rota Bioceânica, ele disse que a principal obra em andamento é uma ponte financiada pelo governo federal e defendeu mais investimentos do estado para atrair empresas.

A proposta inclui a realização de levantamentos e estudos para identificar as necessidades de infraestrutura e criar condições para a instalação de novos empreendimentos.

Décima: Diminuição de moradores em situação de rua

O candidato defendeu uma atuação conjunta entre o governo estadual e as prefeituras. A proposta é ampliar os investimentos em políticas públicas e repassar recursos aos municípios com maior demanda.

Segundo ele, parte das pessoas em situação de rua enfrenta a falta de oportunidades e pode superar essa condição com acesso a políticas sociais e oportunidades de trabalho.

O candidato afirmou que as chamadas mães atípicas também precisam de acolhimento e atendimento. Ele defendeu uma política social voltada às famílias e disse que pretende construir um governo que esteja mais próximo da população e consiga atender às demandas diretamente nos municípios.

Décima primeira: Atendimento à agricultura familiar

O candidato elogiou o trabalho da Polícia Militar Ambiental (PMA), mas defendeu a ampliação da fiscalização, especialmente nos rios. Também afirmou que multas ambientais podem sofrer influência política e disse ser favorável ao agronegócio que respeite o meio ambiente e os trabalhadores.

Entre as propostas, citou a criação de cinco cinturões verdes em Mato Grosso do Sul, com unidades previstas para Três Lagoas, Campo Grande, Dourados e Corumbá, além de uma quinta área ainda não especificada. Segundo ele, a medida pode gerar emprego e renda, reduzir o custo dos alimentos e ampliar a produção local.

O candidato também defendeu o fortalecimento da agricultura familiar e o apoio aos pequenos produtores, que, segundo ele, enfrentam dificuldades para comercializar o que produzem. Ele ainda mencionou a falta de água potável em aldeias indígenas como um problema que precisa de políticas públicas.

“Eu quero falar com você sul-mato-grossense o que a sua vida mudou nesses 20 anos com o último governo que ai está, com esse mesmo grupo político? Vamos pensar diferente. Vamos votar em candidatura que apresenta um projeto mais próximo do seu perfil, porque hoje o que tem ai só atende o rico. Queremos fazer um governo mais organizado, um governo que atenda a nossa redação. O candidato do PT veio aqui e teve vergonha de pedir voto para o presidente Lula. Nós vamos pedir, e eu peço. Vote Lucien Rezende 50, vote para os nossos estaduais e federais 50, vote para o nosso candidato a senador Beto do Movimento, que luta pela agricultura familiar e não tem bens apreendidos pela Justiça. Vote no presidente Lula, que defende a nossa democracia, que defende a nossa soberania e que já fez tanto pelo nosso país. Pela agricultura familiar, pelo minha casa minha vida, pelo luz para todos. É muito trabalho feito. Pedimos voto para reeleição do presidente Lula e sem dúvida nenhuma para Lucien Rezende 50”.

articles.title: Círio 2026: Marinha divulga regras para Romaria Fluvial | G1
articles.standfirst: Inscrição de embarcações é obrigatória e fiscalização terá atuação de 700 militares. Transporte de crianças menores de 7 anos em motos aquáticas está proibido.
articles.summary: Inscrição de embarcações é obrigatória e fiscalização terá atuação de 700 militares. Transporte de crianças menores de 7 anos em motos aquáticas está proibido.
articles.body:
A Marinha do Brasil divulgou , nesta sexta-feira (18), as regras e diretrizes de segurança para a Romaria Fluvial do Círio de Nazaré 2026.

Entre as principais determinações para o evento, estão a obrigatoriedade do uso de coletes salva-vidas e a proibição do transporte de crianças menores de 7 anos em motos aquáticas (jet skis) e embarcações sem cabine habitável.

Quem descumprir as normas estabelecidas pela autoridade marítima poderá ter a embarcação apreendida, além de sofrer sanções administrativas e penais.

Para participar da procissão das águas, todas as embarcações devem, obrigatoriamente, realizar uma inscrição prévia junto à Capitania dos Portos. O processo de fiscalização e ordenamento do tráfego aquático começará bem antes do dia do evento.

O Capitão dos Portos da Amazônia Oriental, Capitão de Mar e Guerra Alexandre Batista Pimentel, detalhou que o processo de fiscalização e ordenamento do tráfego aquático começará bem antes do dia do evento.

"Antes de iniciar, no período da inscrição, nós fazemos uma vistoria em todas essas embarcações maiores, verificando se ela possui toda a documentação, se o condutor está habilitado e a situação de conservação da embarcação," explicou.

Ao todo, cerca de 700 militares da Marinha estarão mobilizados para atuar em todas as fases da Romaria Fluvial, desde o período de inscrições até a fiscalização em tempo real no dia do evento. A estimativa é de que cerca de 400 embarcações participem da homenagem este ano.

O Comandante do 4º Distrito Naval, Vice-Almirante Adriano Marcelino Batista, destacou que o planejamento antecipado tem intuito de garantir a tranquilidade dos romeiros.

"A Capitania divulgou uma série de instruções já no mês de agosto para que todos tomem ciência de como inscrever sua embarcação, como eles vão se cadastrar, seja presencialmente ou através do site," afirmou.

Principais regras de segurança para a Romaria Fluvial:

Coletes salva-vidas: Uso obrigatório em motos aquáticas, rabetas, canoas e botes de alumínio e madeira.

Crianças: Proibido o transporte de menores de 7 anos em motos aquáticas e em embarcações que não possuam cabine habitável.

Lotação: O limite máximo de passageiros de cada embarcação deve ser rigorosamente respeitado.

Equipe de saúde: Barcos de grande porte devem, obrigatoriamente, contar com uma equipe de saúde a bordo (composta por, no mínimo, um enfermeiro e um técnico de enfermagem) e reservar duas vagas para militares da Marinha.

Lista de passageiros: Todas as embarcações devem portar a relação nominal completa de passageiros e tripulantes.

Identificação: Serão distribuídas 260 bandeiras de identificação, sendo 60 delas destinadas especificamente ao controle da frota.

articles.title: Empresa abre vaga de trainee no Ceará com salário de R$ 7,5 mil | G1
articles.standfirst: Vaga é voltada para recém-formados na área de Engenharia.
articles.summary: Vaga é voltada para recém-formados na área de Engenharia.
articles.body:
Empresa abre vaga de trainee no Ceará com salário de R$ 7,5 mil. — Foto: Divulgação

A Solar Coca-Cola abriu uma vaga de trainee no Ceará com salário de R$ 7,5 mil por mês. A oportunidade é para profissionais recém-formados na área de engenharia, e as inscrições podem ser feitas até o dia 28 de setembro pela página do Programa de Trainee .

A iniciativa tem duração de 18 meses e é voltada para profissionais com formação superior em bacharelado, licenciatura ou curso tecnólogo nas áreas de logística, manutenção ou engenharia. A graduação deve ter sido concluída ou estar prevista para conclusão entre janeiro de 2021 e dezembro de 2026.

Os candidatos também precisam ter disponibilidade para trabalhar presencialmente durante todo o período do programa.

Além do salário, a empresa oferece vale-refeição ou refeitório na unidade, vale-transporte ou transporte fretado, plano de saúde, plano odontológico, seguro de vida e participação nos resultados. Dentre os benefícios, o pacote também inclui programa de saúde emocional, telemedicina e plataforma com acesso a rede de academias.

As inscrições são feitas pela internet, no site oficial do Programa de Trainee da Solar Coca-Cola, até 28 de setembro .

Além do Ceará, há oportunidades para a área de Logística em Alagoas e no Maranhão e para a área de Manutenção na Bahia e em Mato Grosso.

A seleção será realizada em etapas entre setembro e janeiro. Após as inscrições, estão previstas entrevistas remotas e vídeo-entrevista em outubro.

Em novembro, os candidatos participam de dinâmicas e novas entrevistas online. Uma etapa presencial está prevista para dezembro. A admissão dos aprovados deve ocorrer em janeiro.

articles.title: Hotel em SC é elevado à  categoria de duas chaves Michelin | G1
articles.standfirst: O Awasi Santa Catarina, em Governador Celso Ramos, subiu de categoria e passou a integrar a seleta lista dos apenas três hotéis brasileiros com duas chaves.
articles.summary: Awasi Santa Catarina, em Governador Celso Ramos, conquista duas chaves no Guia Michelin após hospedar estrelas como Beyoncé e Paul McCartney em seus bangalôs privativos.
articles.body:
Hotel Awasi Santa Catarina, em Governador Celso Ramos (SC) — Foto: Divulgação

O hotel Awasi Santa Catarina, em Governador Celso Ramos , na Grande Florianópolis, foi elevado à categoria de duas chaves Michelin pelo Guia Michelin. A segunda edição da seleção global foi divulgada nesta sexta-feira (18).

Situado em uma área isolada da Costa Esmeralda, o refúgio de luxo já hospedou astros internacionais como Beyoncé , Paul McCartney e Katy Perry . O próprio guia destaca que muitos visitantes chegam ao local de helicóptero particular.

Anteriormente conhecido como Ponta dos Ganchos Exclusive Resort, o estabelecimento já havia conquistado uma chave na primeira edição do guia , publicada no ano passado.

🔑🔑 Além de ser o único representante de Santa Catarina, com a promoção, passou a integrar a seleta lista dos apenas três hotéis brasileiros com duas chaves.

Só uma das 22 propriedades brasileiras no guia tem três chaves.

Diferente dos cenários de grandes resorts do Brasil, não há arranha-céus modernos ao estilo de Copacabana neste trecho do litoral. O espaço conta com apenas 25 bangalôs privativos espalhados pela paisagem natural.

A seleção do Guia Michelin é baseada em cinco critérios universais. A avaliação atribui chaves que consideram a experiência geral de hospitalidade e os serviços individuais oferecidos aos hóspedes.

Conhecido mundialmente pelas estrelas concedidas a restaurantes, o Guia Michelin lançou a classificação voltada para a hotelaria em 2025.

O sistema de chaves segue a mesma lógica das estrelas de restaurantes: quanto mais chaves o estabelecimento recebe, maior é o reconhecimento . A classificação máxima é de três chaves.

Apesar dos bangalôs, não há esteiras de palha ou mosquiteiros rústicos nas acomodações.

Os quartos são elegantes, climatizados e equipados com comodidades modernas. Os lençóis são de algodão egípcio. Lareiras e acesso à internet garantem o conforto interno, enquanto redes e espreguiçadeiras nas varandas privativas permitem apreciar a vista panorâmica para o mar.

Os bangalôs também têm banheiras de hidromassagem no terraço, adegas, piscinas privativas e banheiros duplos espaçosos, com instalações separadas para casais.

articles.title: Iran war sows bitter divisions for diaspora in US
articles.summary: When the war on Iran began seven months ago, Washington area Iranian-American Soroush quickly found himself losing friends."People (in Iran) are going to los...
articles.body:
When the war on Iran began seven months ago, Washington area Iranian-American Soroush quickly found himself losing friends.

He hates the Islamic government in Tehran but believes "nothing is going to be better" by going to war.

Fellow exiles in the United States began accusing him of supporting their oppressors.

Another Iranian-American, Bahar, also found herself being cut off within the diaspora -- but in her case because she strongly supported the war launched by US President Donald Trump.

The 750,000-strong Iranian community in the US is overwhelmingly united in opposing Iran's Islamic regime whose top leadership has been decimated by the US-Israeli offensive that has destroyed swaths of the country's military and prompted global economic shocks.

But deep fault lines have appeared among expatriates and exiles over whether the war will succeed in ending 47 years of clerical rule in their homeland.

"Family relationships have been strained or broken...Even lifelong friendships have ended over this," said Sahar Razavi, director of the Iranian and Middle Eastern Studies Center at California State University, Sacramento, who says the war exacerbated pre-existing tensions.

AFP spoke to Iranian community members around Washington about the tensions. Some requested their full names be withheld as they talked about their own friends and relatives.

Soroush, a 3D artist and animator who came to the US a decade ago, described rifts with close friends and even his own brother and sister-in-law after the war started on February 28.

"People (in Iran) are going to lose friends, family members. They're going to lose their job, their savings," he recalled telling them, citing the negative impacts of past US wars in the Middle East.

"They are the ones who are living it, not the Iranian diaspora," the Christian convert told AFP as he nursed a beer at a Washington bar.

At a downtown coffee shop, Bahar, who works in the medical sector, and Aahoo Sigarchi, who works in a bank, took an opposite view.

They are fueled by outrage over the thousands of protesters killed by Iranian security forces in January 2026 which they say necessitated military action to topple the regime.

"We all have our family, our friends inside Iran, and we are just speaking the words that they can't," said Aahoo, a firm supporter of Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of the late shah of Iran who called for an uprising then rallied support among the diaspora.

"I think we are on the right path with the war, and I believe soon we are going to get to what people are looking for," she said, batting away questions about the failure of the military intervention to unseat the regime.

"To be realistic, we have no other solution," Aahoo said.

The war is deeply unpopular among the wider US population grappling with the knock-on effect of rising fuel prices.

Polling commissioned by the National Iranian American Council, an advocacy group that opposes the war, suggests that support among the Iranian diaspora quickly diminished.

At the start of the war, the community in the US was split about half-and-half, but a second poll a month later found 66.1 percent opposed the war and only 32.7 percent supported it.

Razavi said opponents of the war who were skeptical about externally driven regime-change feel vindicated, but many supporters "have dug their heels in further."

She said there is also a significant minority that switched stance to rally around the Iranian government as it stands up to the United States.

"That's something among Iranian diaspora that I see accelerating," she said.

Mohammad Reza Mousavi, a former Tehran-based journalist who opposes both the war and the regime, detects waning war enthusiasm. And he bristles at the intolerance of those who have advocated for it.

"They can label you very easily with whatever they want if they realize that you're not with them in every respect," he said.

According to Razavi, Iranian community organizations that would host Farsi language classes or Persian poetry readings would be "raked over the coals" for not overtly expressing support for the "liberation struggle."

Pahlavi's supporters say communal pressure is not a one-way street.

Bahar said she has been called a fascist for voting for Trump and lost 100 Instagram followers. She has pulled her eight-year-old son from a school that teaches about Iranian art and music after a teacher kept bringing up the war in class.

But Mousavi was pragmatic about the way the war has shaken up the community.

"At these times of hardships, you understand the people around you," he said. "You understand what sort of people they are."

articles.title: Farmer who voted for Trump says farmers are "all just in survival mode"
articles.summary: Matt Bell said he initially supported Trump's policies but now feels he and other farmers were "sold a bill of goods" that there was a plan to "put America's...
articles.body:
Matt Bell, 52, has been farming for more than half his life in central North Carolina. He grows soybeans, corn and wheat and raises beef cattle on more than 1,000 acres. But Bell, who voted for President Trump, says soaring prices for fuel, fertilizer, and equipment are hurting his farm and leading some of his fellow farmers to consider calling it quits once this growing season ends.

"I've done this 34 years. I have never worried and stressed like I have the last year," Bell told CBS News in an interview on Wednesday at his farm in Kings Mountain, North Carolina.

Bell has been forced to make significant changes to his operation as a result of the high costs. He's shifting some of his acreage, trying to stretch out the lifespan of his equipment and producing his own fertilizer. His children have also opened up a storefront where visitors can pick pumpkins and take hayrides in the fall. But Bell is still feeling the pinch.

"We've cut everything we can cut," he said. "The last several years in agriculture have been terrible, and we have, you know, just cut the fat anywhere we could. But we're just getting to the point now there's nothing left to cut. You cannot run without fuel. You cannot run without fertilizer. You have to have that."

Bell says his diesel fuel costs have about doubled since last year

The war with Iran has driven up fuel costs and created supply chain disruptions as the Strait of Hormuz remains under a naval blockade with a limited number of oil tankers allowed through the critical waterway. And the intensifying conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia and attacks by other Iranian proxy forces on Saudi infrastructure are squeezing global fuel supplies in the Red Sea and contributing to a spike in global fuel costs .

Fighting in Russia and Ukraine has also limited oil refining capacity, driving up prices further.

Diesel prices nationwide are averaging roughly $6.40 per gallon, according to AAA , nearly double the average price a year ago. In North Carolina Thursday, diesel prices hit their highest recorded average of $6.19 per gallon.

Prices have been so volatile that Bell said the price he's quoted from his distributor in the morning is only valid until the afternoon — when it rises again. He can't avoid the expense — his farm equipment runs on diesel. Bell showed CBS News his combine, which he says now requires about $600 worth of diesel fuel per day. That's more than twice what he paid last year.

Bell said he blew through his yearly fuel budget of $35,000 in August. Now, he expects his total for the year to be closer to $50,000 to $60,000.

"Every piece of equipment on this farm runs on diesel," he said. Without it, his farm wouldn't be able to function.

Tariff impact: "Everything that we touch has gone up"

It's not just diesel prices that are hurting Bell's business. President Trump's wide-ranging tariffs have also driven up costs — and left him and other farmers in limbo as the president continues to threaten to impose more tariffs.

"Everything we're touching, the fertilizer, fuel, chemicals, seed, parts — you know, the whole nine yards, everything that we touch has gone up," Bell said, noting that many of the price hikes resulted from Mr. Trump's tariff policies.

Farmers welcomed Mr. Trump's announcement in May that he had reached a deal for China to buy 25 million metric tons of soybeans from the U.S. annually through 2028. China has purchased significantly more U.S. soybeans in 2026 compared to 2025, but its 10% retaliatory tariff on U.S. soybeans remains in place. China imposed the levy in response to Mr. Trump's fentanyl-related tariffs on China.

Bell said China's soybean tariffs have left the market in limbo: That is, China hasn't increased the prices it's paying for U.S. soybeans, even though everything farmers touch in producing soybeans "has gone up."

In a letter to Mr. Trump on Thursday ahead of his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week, the American Soybean Association called on him to push for the elimination of the 10% tariff.

Bell initially supported Mr. Trump's policies and even thought short-term price increases resulting from the Iran conflict would be worth ensuring Iran never has a nuclear weapon, one of the president's stated goals of the war.

But he now says the administration has made miscalculations in the war. "We're just being strung along as a country and that's not good," Bell said.

Bell criticized the administration's decision-making around the war, saying, "I think we've been misled."

He also says the administration's agriculture policy is not what he was promised.

"We were sold a bill of goods that agriculture was going to be on the forefront … and there was going to be some policy that would put America's farmers and ranchers first. And right now, that has not happened."

Bell said that while the administration's farmer bailout program sounds significant, "it's not a lot of money."

This November, Bell says he'll be voting for candidates who he says have "common sense," and listen to Americans' concerns.

"I'm a Republican, but I'm probably going to vote a split ticket," he said.

Bell said he knows farmers who have been forced out of business as a result of high costs, unable to sustain their business with rising prices.

"I do not want any Americans to feel sorry for the American farmer," Bell said. "I want the Americans to be mad that we have been put in this situation. We are fighting for survival, and we're running out of options."

And he acknowledged it's possible he could also be forced to shutter his farm.

"Money's not the problem, I could care less about the money," he said. "But we take a lot of pride in what we do. You can't put a dollar sign on that. But I can't stay in business under these conditions. Something has got to give."

But asked what he would do if he wasn't a farmer, Bell hesitated: "I don't know. It's all I've ever done."

images.caption: North Carolina farmer Matt Bell is interviewed by CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes. / Credit: CBS News
September 2026: North Carolina farmer Matt Bell's equipment runs on diesel fuel, which is about twice as expensive now as it was a year ago.

articles.title: Don't call, do text: Gen Z has a lot of feelings about phone etiquette
articles.summary: When it comes to phone calls, younger generations aren't picking up. They have a lot of feelings about taking — and making — a spontaneous call.
articles.body:
Younger generations simply aren't picking up the phone.

That's OK — they're not doing much calling, either.

How, and when, did spontaneous phone calls become rude?

For the younger generations raised with smartphones , there is one phone feature they often avoid at all costs: the call button.

The ubiquity of smartphones means that ringing someone up has become just one option among many. Now, we can send a text, email, DM, or voice note, and actual calls have fallen out of favor.

Somewhere along the way, making a phone call without warning became less a casual way to catch up and more of an annoyance — or even a sign there's been an emergency. However, spontaneous calls still have their fans, and etiquette experts told Business Insider that they can help foster connection and clarity in real time.

What happened to the spontaneous phone call?

Spontaneous phone calls used to be exactly that: spontaneous . You'd call a friend because you were thinking about them, had a recipe to share, or simply wanted to hear their voice — no appointment required.

But are we missing something by leaving those unplanned conversations behind? Could bringing back the casual check-in call actually be good for our relationships, stress levels, and overall well-being?

For Mary Jane Copps, a communication expert known as the Phone Lady, the shift isn't just about younger generations preferring text messages over phone calls .

Instead, it's a combination of evolving technology, expectations, and the fact that our phones are now always with us. Unlike previous generations, today's phone calls can arrive anytime, anywhere — while someone is working, driving, running errands, or simply taking a break.

"That's the difference of the phone on the wall in the kitchen, you were always at home when you took a phone call," Copps said. "Whereas now you can be anywhere; you can be sleeping, you can be in a meeting, you can be skateboarding."

Still, it's not only that calls can come at inconvenient times. The way we communicate has also changed because we now have endless options with our technology.

"While we call this a phone, it's really a computer with a phone app ," Copps said, holding one up. "With this, I have the choice to text you, to email you, to talk to you on LinkedIn. I don't have to phone you."

The phone call didn't disappear — it simply became one option among many. With texts, DMs, emails, and video calls competing for attention, picking up the phone is no longer the automatic choice it once was.

Why the call button feels like a jump scare

For Cassie Leigh , 30, an unexpected phone call rarely feels casual. Instead, it often feels like a sign that something is wrong. "Whenever I see anybody, especially family, calling me, it feels like an urgent matter, as opposed to just texting. It feels dreadful," she said.

Leigh said texting feels more natural because it gives her time to think before responding. "It gives me the opportunity to take a moment to actually form what I want to say without just blurting something out," she explained.

While she doesn't particularly love phone calls, Leigh isn't against hearing someone's voice altogether. In addition to texts, she likes voice messages because they also don't require an immediate response, and when sending one herself, she can edit what she wants to say.

That desire for more control is part of what makes texting feel so comfortable, said Copps. "When we're texting or emailing, we have time to think, we have time to edit," she added. "It doesn't have to be instantaneous."

Why do some people still want the callback?

For some people, the lack of a script isn't a drawback — it's exactly what makes a phone call feel more personal.

For Maggie Cornejo, 27, phone calls offer something texting cannot. She said she values "the human connection — hearing someone's voice, jokes, and being able to ask follow-up questions."

Working remotely has also made those moments of connection more meaningful to her.

"I am kind of alone all day, every day, not working in an office," Cornejo said. "Having that chatter with a friend that you haven't seen in a while" can feel energizing.

Still, Cornejo considers herself in the minority among her friends when it comes to liking phone calls.

"I have a few special friends where it's an unsaid thing that we call each other and play phone tag, and it's totally fine. But I have some friends that, if I called them out of the blue, they'd be like, 'Oh my gosh, is something wrong?'"

Texting, on the other hand, can sometimes feel like another task to manage, and without tone of voice, it can also leave room for misunderstandings. In some cases, hearing someone's voice can resolve a misunderstanding faster than going back and forth on a screen.

"You're not going to get rid of that confusion by continuing to text or email. It's the sound of your voice that's going to eliminate that confusion," Cornejo said.

So, to call or not to call? For Copps, the answer isn't necessarily to abandon phone calls altogether or expect everyone to pick up every time. Instead, it's about remembering what phone calls can offer that other forms of communication cannot: connection in real time.

Sure, texting can create connection , too, but by comparison, phone conversations allow people to build deeper relationships through empathy, compassion, and the simple act of hearing another person's voice.

However, bringing back phone calls doesn't mean everyone should start calling without consideration. Like any form of communication, etiquette still matters .

Mariah G. Humbert, an etiquette expert and a Gen Zer herself, doesn't necessarily consider an unexpected phone call to be rude. A casual call can still be a thoughtful way to catch up, but certain conversations deserve more consideration, she explained.

"If you are calling someone with the intention of talking about something sensitive, or potentially challenging, that's when you want to think about it being the right place or right time," she said.

That also applies to the now-common "Can I call you?" text. While it may seem polite, the wording can sometimes create as much stress as a spontaneous phone call itself.

"When it's a text to schedule a phone call , that creates a lot of anxiety," Humbert said. Messages like, 'Can I call you later?' or 'I need to discuss something with you' can send the other person into a spiral."

Instead, Humbert suggested giving context about why you want to talk, so they know what to expect. Still, the occasional spontaneous call can be meaningful — especially when it comes from someone you're already close with.

"I encourage people to check in on the people that they're close to for no other reason than to see how they're doing," she said.

Maybe part of getting comfortable with phone calls again is simply allowing yourself to be a little uncomfortable at first. Copps recommended starting small: Call someone who's been on your mind, leave a voicemail, or send a voice message instead of another text.

After all, sometimes the best way to get over this hang-up is to stop overthinking it and just pick up the line.

articles.title: Police clear Ceuta migrants off beaches in Spanish enclave
articles.summary: At least 10,000 of the 72,000 migrants who broke through fence from Morocco in July remain in the Spanish enclave.
articles.body:
Spanish police have started clearing thousands of migrants from the beaches of Ceuta, an enclave on North Africa’s coast which saw a surge of arrivals from neighbouring Morocco in July.

Riot police ‌fired rubber bullets into the air and struck people with batons on Friday ⁠as they began ⁠an operation, which started shortly before 7am local time (05:00 GMT).

More than 72,000 people surged into the 18.5 square kilometre (7.2sq mile) enclave at the end of July in an unprecedented border ⁠rush, although most later left.

Spain estimates 10,000 migrants remain in the tiny territory.

The authorities have built new temporary housing inside Ceuta’s port to hold 1,700 people. NGOs say thousands remain unhoused and have been sleeping rough in camps.

The AFP news agency reported that the new location where some of the migrants are being settled in tents near the port has showers and beds.

Ceuta, with an official population of 80,000 residents, has been in Spanish possession since 1580.

It is one of two Spanish territories on the North African coast, along with Melilla.

Christians and Muslims, Spanish and Moroccan residents and day workers all live there in relative harmony behind a border fence that many migrants from across Africa attempt to cross or swim around for a better life in Europe.

On Friday, EU Migration Commissioner ⁠Magnus Brunner said that images of migrants crossing into ⁠Ceuta have fuelled support for far-right parties despite a sharp decline in irregular arrivals in Europe following tougher migration policies.

“We have the decreasing numbers, but images from Ceuta, of course, overshadow the actual successes and the actual facts and figures,” Brunner told Reuters in an interview.

He said these images “fuel the far right”, which was why “it is so important ‌to return those people as soon as possible to show that we have control”.

Separately on Friday, Spain’s World Cup-winning coach Luis de la Fuente released a video from Ceuta as he announced his Nations League squad in a show of support for the enclave.

articles.title: Russia’s drones threaten Kyiv-bound Western officials as war effort stalls
articles.summary: Russia strikes Ukraine’s border crossings with Poland and Moldova as its offensives peter out in the east.
articles.body:
Russia has threatened the safety of Ukrainian, American and European officials travelling to and from Kyiv using drones.

These attacks have come as Russia’s ground war stumbles.

Details emerged this week of its latest setback when an attempt to seize the city of Lyman resulted in the loss of 85 square kilometres (33 square miles) of territory Russia had previously occupied in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region.

On September 13, Russian drones struck a Ukrainian train locomotive 5km (3 miles) from the border with Poland, endangering European officials travelling to Warsaw after they attended the Yalta European Strategy conference, an annual gathering of global political, business and civil society leaders in Kyiv.

Boris Johnson, Britain’s former premier, and European political and security officials were on the train.

Ukraine’s railway company, Ukraliznytsia, said the locomotive of the passenger train had been struck.

A Russian drone also struck a petrol station 2km (1.2 miles) from the Polish border, destroying or damaging a number of trucks.

Polish premier Donald Tusk said he expects a period of “very intensified actions by Russia”, possibly including an “escalation will also affect our territory”.

“This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said on social media.

In another incident on September 8, a Russian drone entered Moldovan airspace as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s plane prepared to depart Chisinau, delaying the flight. Norway’s prime minister said it nearly struck the aircraft, though Moldova has not confirmed the claim.

On September 6, US diplomatic envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff flew to Poland before taking a train to Kyiv after Russian strikes disrupted flights to the Ukrainian capital.

Russian drones and missiles have also struck four Ukrainian border crossings to Moldova in recent weeks.

Kremlin Ambassador-at-large Rodion Miroshnik said the strikes were justified as part of Russia’s effort to stop Western military aid from reaching Kyiv.

Ukraine has turned its ports, border crossings and logistics centres into “military targets”, he wrote on social media, boasting that Kyiv was “reaping the inevitable consequences”.

Five people were killed on Wednesday when a drone struck their intercity minibus near Nikopol in the northern Kharkiv region in what Zelenskyy called “another act of brutality”.

“Just this week, Russia has launched approximately 2,100 drones at Ukraine,” along with 78 missiles, Zelenskyy said on Sunday.

Hope for more aid came on Thursday, when both houses of the US Congress passed a bill sponsored by Senators Darline Graham and Richard Blumenthal imposing secondary sanctions on countries buying Russian oil and gas.

If implemented, the bill could deprive Russia of export revenues it needs to replenish its budget, one-third of which goes to defence.

Russia has ‘no grand illusions’ on peace

Ukraine has struck 26 Russian refineries this year. In the past week it struck eight, aiming for their desalination and vacuum distillation units that take months to repair.

Numerous reports estimate that Ukraine has deprived Russia of at least 30 percent of its actual refining capacity.

Russian Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina recently said inflation over the summer was “primarily driven by the situation in the fuel market”.

“We continue to assess inflationary risks as predominant and believe they have increased,” she said.

Ukraine has proposed a ceasefire on strikes to energy infrastructure since 2025, but Russia has signalled that it is ready for talks only on its terms. These include surrendering the remaining one-fifth of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region it does not control and a broad demilitarised buffer zone beyond that.

“We have no grand illusions here,” said Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

Kushner told the Yalta European Strategy conference this week that an agreement between the US and Russia was largely prepared, claiming Ukraine’s refusal to surrender the remainder of Donetsk was the main obstacle.

Over the past week, Ukrainian drones also set fire to the Tolyattikauchuk synthetic rubber factory in Samara near the border with Kazakhstan. The rubber is used in the production of solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles.

Ukraine also struck the Atlant Aero factory in Taganrog, which builds Molnya reconnaissance and attack drones and makes parts for Orion drones. On September 17, Ukraine struck an Antonov-12 and two Antonov-26 military transport aircraft on the tarmac at Rostov air base near the southern Ukrainian border and also destroyed three helicopters.

Russia has been repeatedly frustrated in its efforts to seize the “fortress belt” of cities in Donetsk – Sloviansk, Kramatorsk and Druzhivka. Putin’s December 31 deadline for achieving this is his 15th of the war.

Russian forces have tried to outflank the fortress belt from the north by seizing the cities of Lyman and Svyatohirsk to its northeast, said brigadier-general Andriy Biletskyi, commander of the Third Army Corps defending the area.

A separate offensive was from the south, he said.

The southern flanking movement was defeated in August this year, taking back 745 sq km (290 sq miles) of territory around Dobropillya.

Ukraine also pushed back in Lyman and retook 85 sq km (53 square miles) of territory, its Third Army Corps revealed this week.

“The northern pincer has effectively been defeated and destroyed,” Biletskyi said.

“Over the space of several months, Ukraine has executed two quiet yet successful counteroffensive operations in different parts of the country,” noted military strategist Mick Ryan, a former Australian army general. “Ukrainians have been investing in the hard intellectual work of finding new methods of conducting successful offensive action at the tactical and operational levels.”

Ukraine’s military said Russian losses in 2026 crossed the 300,000 threshold over the past week, with 20,360 casualties for the first half of September, putting Russia on track for over 40,000 casualties for the month – higher than its reported recruitment rate.

Al Jazeera cannot independently verify casualty claims by either side.

Ukraine’s chief of military intelligence said Russian generals have asked Putin for 800,000 troops above normal recruitment levels.

articles.title: Mexico’s Sheinbaum says she spoke with Trump as trade negotiations continue
articles.summary: Mexican president says she is seeking a decrease in tariffs as both countries seek new bilateral trade deal.
articles.body:
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has said that she had a “very good” phone call with United States counterpart Donald Trump, as the neighbouring countries continue to work towards an agreement on a bilateral trade deal.

Speaking during her morning news conference on Friday, the Mexican president said that she spoke with Trump on Wednesday but did not provide additional details.

“Progress is being made toward a potential agreement between us, Mexico, and the United States,” Sheinbaum said, adding that she hopes the deal will result in a decrease in US tariffs on Mexican products.

“We are doing everything we can, within the framework of sovereignty, respect, and what is best for Mexico, to reach a deal soon,” she added.

Mexico and the US are seeking a bilateral trade deal before the November midterm elections in the US, where many voters attribute higher prices in part to Trump’s imposition of steep import taxes on most trading partners around the world.

Sheinbaum said that Mexico hopes to obtain tariff relief for industries such as steel, aluminium, and cars.

Mexico and Canada are part of a free trade agreement with the US – known as the USMCA – that has created a high degree of economic integration over the last several decades and exempted the majority of exports from US tariffs.

But Trump slapped some of those industries with high tariffs. As a result, Mexico and Canada are now among those scrambling to adjust to the Trump administration’s efforts to reorient US trade relations.

In remarks on Thursday, Trump said he could end trade relations with Mexico and European countries in response to a decision by the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.

Efforts to reach an agreement between Mexico and the US also come amid escalating tensions between the US and Canada, which have prompted both sides to step up tariffs on some of their respective products.

Comments from Trump have also brought anger in both neighbouring countries for what critics see as blatant disregard for their sovereignty.

Trump has mused about turning Canada into the 51st state and pushed for US military operations on Mexican territory, remarks that have prompted unease and pushback from Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

articles.title: Nearly 30 years later, Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ goes up for auction
articles.summary: Diana wore the dress the same day a TV interview aired in which Charles acknowledged his affair.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Princess Diana’s iconic “revenge dress” is going up for auction — nearly three decades after she made headlines wearing it.

The striking black dress , worn by Diana on the night her then-husband , King Charles III, publicly acknowledged his infidelity, is being offered by Sotheby’s with a presale estimate of $150,000 to $300,000.

The dress went on public display Friday in London as it begins an international tour ahead of its December auction in New York.

Diana wore the figure-hugging, off-the-shoulder silk dress by Greek designer Christina Stambolian to a gala at London’s Serpentine Gallery on June 29, 1994 — the same day a television interview aired in which Charles acknowledged his affair.

Morgane Halimi, Sotheby’s global head of handbags and fashion, said Diana used fashion to express herself and reclaim control of her own story.

Images of her wearing the dress, paired with a sapphire necklace, black pumps and bright red nail polish, quickly spread around the world. The following day, The Sun famously declared: “Revenge is chic.”

The dress became one of the most recognizable looks associated with Diana, known for her fashion influence and was among the world’s most photographed women.

The “people’s princess” later acknowledged the affair during a 1995 interview, famously saying, “There were three of us in this marriage,” referring to Charles’s relationship with Camilla Parker-Bowles, now Queen Camilla.

Charles and Diana divorced in 1996. The Princess of Wales was killed in a Paris car crash the following year at age 36.

The dress is being auctioned for the first time since 1997, when Diana sold it along with other clothing to raise money for AIDS charities.

Sotheby’s expects the dress could sell for significantly more than its presale estimate. In 2023, a red sweater featuring a sheep design that Diana wore to a polo match sold for $1.1 million, setting a record for an item owned by the late princess.

The “revenge dress” will remain on display in London through Sept. 24 before traveling to Hong Kong and Geneva. It will then be offered at auction in New York on Dec. 9.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: UK harbour moved dredged mud onto a damaged saltmarsh; within one winter, vegetation began returning
articles.summary: UK News: A trial at Lymington Harbour in Hampshire has shown how sediment dredged from the harbour could be reused to help restore an eroding saltmarsh, with v.
articles.body: A trial at Lymington Harbour in Hampshire has shown how sediment dredged from the harbour could be reused to help restore an eroding saltmarsh, with vegetation returning to a treated area within about a year. The project is being led by Lymington Harbour Commissioners with Land & Water and other partners, including the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Wildlife Trust, the Environment Agency and the Crown Estate. Lymington's saltmarsh has been declining since around 1920 and continues to erode, raising concerns about the natural coastal protection it provides around the harbour. Instead of allowing dredged sediment to remain in conventional disposal areas, the project has tested ways of moving it to higher parts of the marsh, where the ground can reach elevations suitable for saltmarsh vegetation to establish. After the first 2024 trial, around 800 cubic metres of sediment had been placed, and monitoring showed substantial vegetation recovery by the following year.The project moves dredged sediment to a higher part of the marshLymington Harbour has already been using dredged sediment as part of efforts to slow saltmarsh erosion. Since 2014, Lymington Harbour Commissioners have been able to place up to 10,000 wet tonnes of dredged sediment a year in a licensed disposal area near Boiler Marsh. Surveys by August 2023 showed that this sediment had built up an area of around 17,000 square metres by about 1.5 metres, helping reduce erosion of the marsh behind it. However, the material remained too low in the tidal frame for new high saltmarsh to establish.The new restoration project was designed to solve that problem by moving already deposited sediment onto lower-lying areas of deteriorating marsh. A first trial was carried out in August and September 2024 using a Saltmarsh Restoration Drag Box developed for moving sediment in shallow intertidal environments. The Marine Management Organisation had granted Lymington Harbour Commissioners a 10-year licence in December 2023 to trial new techniques, while the Environment Agency provided funding from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Water Improvement Fund.The first trial faced problems but vegetation returned quicklyThe 2024 campaign did not move as much sediment as originally intended. Difficult ground conditions contributed to equipment problems, while an unseasonably windy period also affected the operation. Even so, the project team considered the technique promising and used the experience to improve subsequent work. The trial area continued to be monitored through 2025.The ecological response was more encouraging. About 800 cubic metres of sediment were placed in the first trial area at an elevation intended to support saltmarsh regeneration. When the team returned around 12 months later, they found good-quality saltmarsh vegetation growing there. Project representatives said the material had been rapidly colonised, with the transformation occurring over a single winter. The restoration relies on reaching a suitable elevation and providing sediment with appropriate physical and chemical characteristics, after which seeds carried by wind and birds can naturally establish on the surface.Lymington has lost much of its saltmarsh over the past centuryThe restoration is taking place against a long-term decline in Lymington's saltmarsh. The Crown Estate says the area has lost around 85% of its saltmarsh over the past 100 years. The harbour's saltmarsh provides coastal protection while also supporting wildlife, including birds and other species associated with intertidal habitats.The problem extends beyond Lymington. Dr Jonathan Dale, a physical geography lecturer at the University of Reading who studies wetland restoration, said the decline has reduced benefits including carbon storage, flood defence and habitat for fish and birds. Dale also noted that traditional managed realignment, which involves breaching existing flood defences to allow tidal water onto land behind them, is not suitable everywhere, particularly where infrastructure or heritage assets occupy the land behind existing defences.Researchers hope the approach can be used elsewhereThe Lymington project is now being developed beyond the initial trial. A second phase has allowed the team to move a larger quantity of sediment more efficiently, while continuing to test how dredged material can be placed at elevations suitable for saltmarsh restoration. The Crown Estate has backed the work as part of its wider interest in finding ways to combine harbour maintenance with nature restoration.Dale said the Lymington trial could provide another option for restoring saltmarsh in locations where conventional approaches are unsuitable. He pointed to projects using brushwood structures in the Dart and Severn estuaries, which trap sediment and encourage marsh development, but said the use of dredged sediment could offer an additional restoration method. The Lymington team similarly hopes that lessons from the trial can be applied to other eroding saltmarshes around the UK, although further monitoring will be needed to establish how durable the restored habitat is over the longer term.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Scottish Sikh gets bail in 7 NIA cases after 8 years behind bars
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI/LONDON/BATHINDA: Delhi HC on Friday granted bail to British citizen Jagtar Singh Johal, who is charged with targeted killings and conspiracy.
articles.body: NEW DELHI/LONDON/BATHINDA: Delhi HC on Friday granted bail to British citizen Jagtar Singh Johal, who is charged with targeted killings and conspiracy linked to Khalistan Liberation Force (KLF), taking note of his “long period of incarceration” and acquittal in one of the cases. News of his bail sparked celebrations at his home in Dumbarton, Scotland, and among UK-based activists who have been campaigning for his release.His brother Gurpreet Singh Johal, a solicitor in Dumbarton, where Johal’s wife Gurpreet Kaur Johal also lives, said, “The past two years have been an expensive rollercoaster, contesting bails at Supreme Court and back to the high court in India. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison. We have waited so long and fought so hard for this moment. Whenever evidence against Jagtar is tested in court, judges find what we’ve said all along, which is that there isn’t any.”Johal’s MP Douglas McAllister, who has been campaigning for his release, described the news as “amazing”. “Now it’s time to bring him home.”Scotland-born Johal, arrested shortly after his 2017 wedding, was named as an accused in eight cases of attempted murder in Punjab and booked by NIA under UAPA. He was acquitted in one of the cases last year.HC heard Johal’s bail appeals in the remaining seven case together Friday and said, “We find the appellant has remained in custody for more than eight years… Only 40 witnesses have so far been examined and we are informed there are another 123 witnesses whose testimony is yet to be recorded... Trial is certainly not likely to conclude any time soon.”On NIA’s claim Johal was a flight risk as a foreign national, HC ordered Johal to surrender his passport and barred him from joining any WhatsApp group or other social media platform where anti-national material was uploaded or circulated or propagated.It rejected NIA’s claim certain witnesses alleged they were threatened and that, if released, Johal might influence the trial.NIA’s cases against Johal arise from a series of allegedly targeted murders and attempted murders in Ludhiana and Jalandhar in 2016-2017. Two cases pertain to the killing of Amit Sharma, president of Shri Hindu Takhat in Ludhiana in Jan 2017, and the attempted murder of Jagdish Kumar Gagneja, RSS vice-president in Punjab, in Jalandhar in Aug 2016.The probe was transferred from Punjab Police to NIA after the offences were identified to be a part of a “transnational conspiracy”. NIA accused Johal of being an “active member” of the “terrorist gang” KLF.Gurpreet Singh Johal told BBC News, “We are still waiting for the order and a report. We expect he won’t be allowed to leave India without permission... But at last we see some light at the end of the tunnel that he will be at least at liberty.”Noting Johal was acquitted of all charges in one case, he said, “Jagtar is innocent and is arbitrarily detained. There is a lot more that has to be done from UK govt. They have not done enough.”Dan Dolan, deputy executive director of Reprieve, a UK legal rights organisation campaigning for Johal’s release, said, “While this judgment is welcome as Jagtar should not be in prison a day longer, we must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way.”Chris Esdaile, senior legal adviser at REDRESS, a London NGO that pursues legal claims on behalf of survivors of torture around the world that also campaigned for Johal, said, “This is a welcome development but it can’t undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention without a fair and timely resolution.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Lane Kiffin's visit to Oxford isn't the first time a coach made an unwelcome return to his former school
articles.summary: Lane Kiffin's return to Ole Miss headlines a history of hostile SEC homecomings, from Nick Saban at Death Valley to mustard bottles at Neyland Stadium.
articles.body: By now, most of you are painfully aware of the game taking place in Oxford, Mississippi, this weekend between LSU and Ole Miss. It's less of a game and more a national event, given the added stakes of Tigers head coach Lane Kiffin making his return to Vaught Hemingway Stadium for the first time since leaving the Rebels in the lurch to make his way to Baton Rouge. There will be plenty of bad blood to go around for all parties involved, but this kind of "reunion" isn't entirely unprecedented. Prominent head coaches will, occasionally, leave their teams on less than ideal terms, and when they make the return trip to the place they used to call home, it can get a little toxic. With that in mind, I decided to take a look at a few other times head coaches made their way back to the schools that used to employ them and how those trips compared to Kiffin's welcome committee in Oxford. MOUNTED POLICE, EXTRA PATROLS AND KIFFIN HATE: OXFORD PREPARES FOR OLE MISS-LSU GAME WITH EXTRA SECURITY Some of these went a little more amicably than others, but all were fairly noteworthy, so let's dive in. 2008 Alabama vs. LSU: Nick Saban's triumphant return to Death Valley Before he became the unquestioned GOAT in the annals of college football, Nick Saban was a wildly successful coach at LSU in the early to mid-2000s. After a pair of SEC Championships and a national title during his five-year tenure with the Tigers, Saban departed for the NFL, leaving many folks on the bayou feeling embittered and betrayed. Following an unremarkable pair of seasons with the Miami Dolphins, Saban decided it was time to return to the college ranks, opting to don the headset at LSU's biggest rival, Alabama, in 2007. OLE MISS AND LSU WILL DELIVER CINEMA, BUT THE NEXT WEEK FOR EACH TEAM COULD BE THEIR MOST PIVOTAL TESTS Tiger fans would only have to wait one year before their former head coach made his way back to Death Valley, as the top-ranked Crimson Tide made their way to Baton Rouge to play 15th-ranked LSU. The atmosphere around the game was tense and filled with anger and resentment toward Saban, and it didn't help that the Tide escaped with a 27-21 overtime win to effectively knock the Bayou Bengals out of the SEC Championship hunt. Saban was given a police escort out of the stadium, and years later, the six-time national champion would call leaving LSU the biggest mistake of his career. 2006 South Carolina vs. Florida: The Swamp claims Head Ball Coach as its latest victim Throughout the entirety of the 90s and into the early 2000s, Steve Spurrier and Florida football were synonymous with one another. The Head Ball Coach won a Heisman Trophy in 1966 while quarterbacking the Gators, and when he returned to roam the sidelines in 1990, he fulfilled the prophecy of "awakening the sleeping giant" once uttered by Alabama legend Paul "Bear" Bryant. Six SEC Championships and one national title later, and Spurrier figured he had accomplished all he needed to, leaving the friendly confines of The Swamp - the name he gave to Ben Hill Griffin Stadium - for an NFL coaching gig with the Washington Redskins in 2002. Much like Nick Saban, Spurrier wasn't long for the pros, returning to the SEC in 2005 as the head coach of the South Carolina Gamecocks. This didn't sit well with a majority of Gator fans, seeing their visor-clad Messiah coaching an SEC East rival, and it made it even worse that he beat his old school in his first year on the job. When Spurrier and the Gamecocks made their first trip to The Swamp together in 2006, a game with national championship implications for the home team had new stakes attached to it. While the fans weren't openly hostile towards their former coach (most were even downright warm), it felt almost like watching a weird alternate reality simulation for those in attendance. The game was an instant classic, with Gators defensive end Jarvis Moss blocking a potential game-winning field goal to preserve the 17-16 win for Florida, and keep their BCS title game hopes alive in the process. Spurrier once said "only Gators get out alive" when referring to The Swamp, and that very phrase came back to bite him on that day in November 2006. 2021 Ole Miss vs. Tennessee: French's and FORE at Neyland Stadium Hey, look! A familiar face! Yes, Lane Kiffin is no stranger to making his way back to old stomping grounds, as he had to do something similar just a few years ago. When Tennessee hired Kiffin in 2009, the then-33-year-old was fresh off of a failed stint as the Oakland Raiders' head coach, and was looking to make a splash in the SEC. A "splash" is putting it mildly, as Kiffin immediately went into prison survival mode and tried to pick a fight with the biggest guy in the pen, that being Florida and head coach Urban Meyer. Kiffin ruffled feathers, accusing Meyer of recruiting violations and promising to "sing Rocky Top all night long" after beating the Gators in The Swamp, but after a year of empty promises and a 7-6 campaign, the brash offensive genius left for sunny Southern California to coach the USC Trojans. Vols fans revolted, burning couches and rioting on campus, while Kiffin left under cover of darkness. Flash forward to 2021, and Tennessee fans finally got their chance to let their old head coach know how they really felt in person, as the Rebels made their way to Neyland Stadium. Kiffin had bounced around as an offensive coordinator and head coach at a few different stops before settling into Oxford to coach the Ole Miss football team, and a night game in Knoxville presented an opportunity for some madness. The game was crazy enough on its own, as the two teams combined for nearly 1,000 yards of total offense and the Vols even had the ball trailing by only five with only a minute left in the fourth quarter. A controversial review then led to a nearly 20 minute delay, as Volunteer fans chucked mustard bottles and golf balls onto the field, the latter of which allegedly hit Kiffin. As he was being interviewed on the field following the win, Kiffin did his best George Costanza impression, presenting the very golf ball that struck him to a shocked ESPN audience watching at home. The fact that this game took place nearly a dozen years after his departure did nothing to snuff out the anger Vols fans held toward their former head coach. 2022 Missouri State vs. Arkansas: Bobby Petrino rides back into Fayetteville Here's one that a lot of people may have forgotten about, but it deserves mention all the same. The first three instances on this list are comprised of coaches who decided to stay in conference and take jobs with rival SEC programs, but what happens when a coach who made an unceremonious exit just happens to be on the schedule by way of a cupcake matchup scheduled years before he even agreed to take the job? CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For those who need a history lesson, Bobby Petrino coached the Arkansas Razorbacks in the late 2000s and early 2010s, even leading the team to a Sugar Bowl berth in 2010 and a top-five finish in 2011. He was incredibly successful in the short time he called Fayetteville home until 2012, when he crashed his motorcycle with a former Arkansas volleyball player riding on the back. This led to an investigation and, eventually, his termination from the university, ending a promising rise for the Razorbacks under Petrino. A decade later, Petrino found his way back to Frank Broyles Field by way of coaching the Missouri State Bears, a lower-end FCS school. Arkansas, conversely, was ranked in the top 10 and looked to improve upon their nine-win season in 2021 with third-year head coach Sam Pittman. It appeared as though the Hogs were going to exact some revenge on their motorcycle-obsessed outcast, but, in a game that may have been a precursor to how the rest of the Pittman era would go, the Razorbacks needed to score 21 unanswered points in the fourth quarter to eke out a 38-27 victory. Petrino would actually go on to be the offensive coordinator for Pittman just one year later, and would even be the interim head coach in 2025 when Pittman was given the axe. They truly can't quit the one that got away in Fayetteville.
